0.title: The Hosts of Heaven
0.essay:
Every December angels appear everywhere: on cards, on the tops of trees, in shop windows. Most are gentle and small; some are chubby babies with tiny wings. The angels of the Bible are rather different. When one of them appears, strong men fall to the ground, and the first words he says are nearly always “Do not be afraid.”

A world larger than we see

The Bible teaches that there is more to the universe than we can see. Around the throne of God, and busy in his service across the earth, are created spirits of great power and holiness. Scripture calls them angels, hosts, holy ones. They worship God, carry his messages and serve his people in ways we rarely notice.

Our age is oddly divided about them. Many people who never pray still believe in angels; many others smile at the idea as a fairy tale. The Bible is neither sentimental nor sceptical. It speaks of angels plainly, as real as the people they visit, and tells us little more than we need. And its angels never want attention: every one of them points away from himself, to God, and in the end to Jesus Christ.

Where this study fits

The study Spiritual Warfare looks at the devil and the fallen angels, their tactics and Christ’s victory over them; The Providence of God at how God governs all things; and Creation & the Fall at the beginning of the world. This study goes deeper into the holy angels: what they are, how they worship, what they have done in the story of salvation, how they serve believers, why they must never be worshipped, and their part at the end.

Why it matters

Thinking about angels is no detour from Christ. Hebrews opens by comparing the Son with the angels, and its point is this: the highest beings God ever made bow before a man who bears the marks of nails. The better we see how great the angels are, the better we can measure how great he is. And the more we see what they have never been given, the more we will marvel at what has been given to us.

The chapters

What Angels Are; Worship Around the Throne; Messengers in the Story of Salvation; Ministering Spirits; Not Angels, but the Offspring of Abraham; “Worship God”: Christ Far Above the Angels; and Innumerable Angels in Festal Gathering.

For reflection

Where do your own pictures of angels come from: Scripture, art, films or Christmas cards? Do you tend to ignore the unseen world, or to be curious about it? What would it change if you remembered that heaven’s greatest servants worship Jesus?

1.title: What Angels Are
1.essay:
The Hebrew word mal’ak and the Greek angelos both mean “messenger”. Augustine observed that “angel” is the name of their work, not of their nature. Ask what they are, and the answer is spirits. Ask what they do, and the answer is messengers.

Made, not gods

First, angels are creatures. The psalmist calls the whole universe to praise God, and the angels head the list: “Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts!” (Psalm 148:2). Then he gives the reason: “Let them praise the name of the LORD! For he commanded and they were created” (Psalm 148:5). However bright they are, they exist only because God spoke.

Paul tells us who did the making. Of the Son he says, “For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Colossians 1:16), and he names the unseen ranks of heaven among the things the Son made. Stop over that for a moment. The angels who sang over the fields of Bethlehem had been made by the baby lying in the manger.

Scripture does not say exactly when they were made, though many have reasoned from Exodus 20:11 that it was within the six days. Job tells us they were there when God laid the earth’s foundations, “when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7). The first thing the angels did on record was to sing.

Spirits, mighty and holy

Angels are “ministering spirits” (Hebrews 1:14). They have no bodies of their own, though they can appear in human form so convincingly that Lot took two of them into his house (Genesis 19:1–3), and “some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2).

They are strong: “Bless the LORD, O you his angels, you mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word!” (Psalm 103:20). They are holy: Jesus speaks of “the holy angels” (Mark 8:38), and Paul of “the elect angels” (1 Timothy 5:21). The Westminster Confession, citing that verse, teaches that God chose angels as well as people for everlasting life: the angels who stood will never fall.

Yet they are not God. They do not know everything: of the day of Christ’s return “no one knows, not even the angels in heaven” (Mark 13:32). They are not everywhere: one angel tells Daniel he was held up for three weeks on his errand (Daniel 10:13).

And there are a great many of them. Daniel saw the throne of God and said, “a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10). John heard “the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands” (Revelation 5:11). These are not counts. They are the language of people who tried to count and gave up.

Cherubim, seraphim, Michael and Gabriel

The Bible gives us only glimpses of their kinds and ranks. Cherubim guard the holiness of God. They were set at the east of Eden “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24); golden cherubim spread their wings over the mercy seat on the ark; and cherubim were woven into the curtain that hid the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31). Ezekiel saw them as living creatures of awesome strangeness (Ezekiel 10). Seraphim, whose name probably means “burning ones”, appear only once, in Isaiah’s vision of the throne (Isaiah 6).

Only two angels are named in the Bible. Michael is “the archangel” (Jude 9) and “the great prince who has charge of your people” (Daniel 12:1). Gabriel is the messenger who says, “I stand in the presence of God” (Luke 1:19). Raphael, who appears in the book of Tobit, belongs to the Apocrypha, which this commentary does not receive as Scripture.

Not people who have died

It is often said, kindly, that someone who has died has “become an angel”. Scripture never says so. Jesus said that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven” (Mark 12:25): like them in that one respect, not turned into them. Hebrews lists “innumerable angels” and “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” as two different companies in heaven (Hebrews 12:22–23). Believers who die remain human, waiting for the resurrection of the body, and they are something no angel has ever been: children of God by adoption, brothers and sisters of the Son.

How little we are told, and why

Around AD 500 a writer who called himself Dionysius the Areopagite arranged the angels into nine orders, and the Middle Ages built a great deal on his scheme. John Calvin warned that such writings were full of clever talk Scripture does not support, and that we should not try to know more about angels than God has revealed. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (Deuteronomy 29:29).

God has told us what we need: that angels exist, that they serve him and us, and that they are not to be worshipped or sought out. He has not told us their ranks or most of their names, and the silence is a kindness. Even in what he leaves unsaid, God is pointing us past the angels to himself.

An example

A girl of thirteen, a few months after her grandmother’s funeral, asked her youth leader whether Gran was now an angel watching over her. The leader opened Hebrews 12, showed her the two companies in heaven, and explained that Gran had not become something other than human, but was with Christ, waiting to be raised. “So she’s still Gran?” the girl asked. “Still Gran,” said the leader. “And one day you will see her face again.”

For reflection

What difference does it make that angels are creatures, made by the Son? Which of the things Scripture tells us about angels surprised you most? Why might God have told us so little about them? How would you gently answer someone who says that a loved one has become an angel?

2.title: Worship Around the Throne
2.essay:
If you could look through the “door standing open in heaven” that John saw (Revelation 4:1), what would you find the angels doing? Not running errands to earth, but worshipping. Before they are messengers to us, they are worshippers of God, and their worship has much to teach ours.

Isaiah in the temple

Isaiah was given a glimpse in the year King Uzziah died. “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew” (Isaiah 6:1–2).

Look at those wings. Two cover the face: sinless creatures, and yet they cannot look full on the glory of God. Two cover the feet, as creatures who know their place. Two are for flying, ready to go the moment they are sent. Reverence, humility and readiness: that is the shape of angelic worship.

Then the song: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!” (Isaiah 6:3). Hebrew repeats a word to make it stronger. No other quality of God is ever raised to the third degree like this. The foundations of the thresholds shook at their voice.

Isaiah’s response was terror: “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). If the seraphim hide their faces, what is a sinful man to do? Then one of the seraphim flew to him with a burning coal from the altar, touched his lips and said, “your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for” (Isaiah 6:7). The angel’s hand carried atonement from the altar to the sinner. Worship that began in holiness ended in grace.

Whose glory did Isaiah see?

After quoting Isaiah, John says, “Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41), and he means Jesus. The one before whom the seraphim cover their faces is the Son. Now read the night of his trial, when some “began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him” (Mark 14:65). The seraphim cover their own faces before him. Men covered his face in contempt. He let them, because he had come to take away the guilt that made Isaiah cry out. The coal from the altar pointed ahead to the sacrifice he would make of himself.

Around the throne in Revelation

John saw the same throne. Of the four living creatures, drawn from Isaiah’s seraphim and Ezekiel’s cherubim, he says that “day and night they never cease to say, ‘Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!’” (Revelation 4:8). They have never grown tired of it. That is not the repetition of the bored. It is the repetition of the endlessly astonished, who look again at God and find each time that the word is still true and still not big enough.

Then the Lamb who was slain takes the scroll no one else was worthy to open, and the angels join in: “the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!’” (Revelation 5:11–12). Notice what they praise: that he “was slain”. The angels have never sinned and never needed a Saviour, and yet what most moves them to worship is the cross.

A choir in a field

They sang once on earth, to a strange audience: not a palace, but a field of shepherds on the night shift. “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!’” (Luke 2:13–14). Heaven’s choir came down because heaven’s King had come down.

Things into which angels long to look

Peter says the gospel preached to ordinary believers concerns “things into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12). The verb pictures someone stooping to peer in. It is the same word John uses of the disciples bending to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5). The angels have seen the world made and the face of God, and they are still bending down to look at what he has done in saving sinners. Through the church “the manifold wisdom of God” is being made known “to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3:10). An ordinary church meeting in a rented hall is being watched by heaven, and heaven is learning about God from it.

What their worship teaches ours

Their worship is centred on God. It is reverent: they cover their faces, and Hebrews calls us to “offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe” (Hebrews 12:28). It is joyful: they shout and sing. It is unceasing, because God never stops being worth it. Every congregation that sings “Holy, holy, holy” is borrowing the seraphim’s words; the study Worship & the Lord’s Day shows how gathered worship joins theirs.

And there is one thing we can sing that they cannot. The angels can say that the Lamb was slain. Only a sinner can say, with Paul, that the Son of God “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). The angels look into salvation from outside. We sing it from inside.

An example

A man in his forties told his pastor he found church boring: the same songs, the same words, every week. The pastor asked him to read Revelation 4 and 5 slowly, and to ask why the living creatures never tire of saying the same thing. Weeks later he said the problem had not been the repetition. He had been singing about a God he hardly ever stopped to look at.

For reflection

What do the six wings of the seraphim teach you about worship? How does it change your view of your church to know that angels long to look into the gospel it preaches? What can you sing that the angels cannot?

3.title: Messengers in the Story of Salvation
3.essay:
Open the Bible at its great turning points and you will find angels standing there: at Sinai, at the birth of Jesus, at his empty tomb, at his ascension. But a herald is never the king, and the angels always pointed beyond themselves.

The law given through angels

Exodus does not mention angels at the giving of the law, but later Scripture does. Stephen said Israel “received the law as delivered by angels” (Acts 7:53). Paul says it “was put in place through angels by an intermediary” (Galatians 3:19), and Hebrews calls it “the message declared by angels” (Hebrews 2:2).

The point is surprising. These verses do not exalt the law by mentioning angels; they mark that it came at one remove, through angels and through Moses. Hebrews goes straight on: “how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord” (Hebrews 2:3). The law came by servants; the gospel by the Son in person.

The angel of the LORD

In the Old Testament one figure stands apart: “the angel of the LORD”, who speaks and acts as God. He finds Hagar in the desert and promises, “I will surely multiply your offspring” (Genesis 16:10), and she calls “the name of the LORD who spoke to her, ‘You are a God of seeing’” (Genesis 16:13). He appears to Moses in the burning bush, and the voice from the bush says, “I am the God of your father” (Exodus 3:6). When Manoah asks his name, he answers, “Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?” (Judges 13:18), using a word closely related to the one in Isaiah’s promise that the child would be called “Wonderful Counselor” (Isaiah 9:6).

Some Christians read him as a created angel, perhaps the chief of them, speaking in God’s name as an ambassador speaks in the first person for his king. That is a serious reading, and it does justice to the fact that he is sent. This commentary’s view: he is best read as the Son himself, appearing before his incarnation. The strongest reason is worship. Created angels refuse it (Revelation 22:9), but the commander of the LORD’s army lets Joshua fall on his face and tells him, “Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy” (Joshua 5:15). And once the Son is born in Bethlehem, this figure who speaks as God no longer appears: the New Testament’s “angel of the Lord” never speaks as God or accepts worship, and is a created servant, as Gabriel is. So this study keeps the two apart: the angel of the LORD who is God the Son, and the angels whom he made.

Gabriel, centuries apart

Gabriel came to Daniel “in swift flight at the time of the evening sacrifice” (Daniel 9:21) with the vision of the seventy weeks, which looked ahead to an anointed one. Some five centuries later, while the old priest Zechariah was offering incense, the same messenger stood by the altar and said, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news” (Luke 1:19). Daniel had been told to wait. Now the same angel came back to say the waiting was nearly over.

Six months later Gabriel went to Nazareth, to a young woman of no rank at all. He told Mary that her son would be called “the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32). The angel who stands in God’s presence announced that the One in whose presence he stands was about to become a child in her womb.

Gethsemane, the tomb and the ascension

In Gethsemane “there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43): the Lord of angels, in his true humanity, strengthened by his creature. At his arrest, he told the disciple who drew a sword to put it away: “Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53). He could have called them. He did not. Every one of those legions stood still while he went to the cross.

On the third day “an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it” (Matthew 28:2). He did not roll it away to let Jesus out. He rolled it away to let the witnesses in. “He is not here, for he has risen, as he said” (Matthew 28:6). Mary Magdalene saw “two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet” (John 20:12). Many readers have been reminded of the two cherubim at either end of the mercy seat, gazing down at the place where the blood was sprinkled. Whether or not John intends the echo, angels again keep watch over the place of atonement.

Forty days later, as the disciples stared after their ascending Lord, two men in white robes said, “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). The angels’ last announcement in the story of Jesus is a promise: he is coming back.

Messengers, not the message

In Acts an angel appears to the Roman officer Cornelius, but does not preach the gospel to him. He tells him to send for a man: “And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter” (Acts 10:5). An angel can announce a birth or an empty tomb, but God has given the preaching of the gospel to forgiven sinners. The angels would have run to do it. He gave it to us.

An example

A long-serving Sunday school teacher admitted he had always envied the shepherds, who heard the news from angels. Acts 10 turned it round for him: heaven had sent an angel to fetch a preacher. He went back to his class of eight-year-olds feeling honoured.

For reflection

Why does Hebrews contrast the law given through angels with the salvation “declared at first by the Lord”? What reasons can you see for reading the angel of the LORD as the Son? Why might God give the gospel to human messengers rather than to angels?

4.title: Ministering Spirits
4.essay:
Hebrews ends its first chapter with a question that expects the answer yes: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14). All of them, even those who stand nearest the throne, are sent to serve people like us.

The great serving the small

The order of things is startling. The angels are “greater in might and power” than we are (2 Peter 2:11), yet God sends them to serve us. Jesus said of the little ones in his church that “in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). The most honoured servants of the court are given charge of the least of its children.

The Psalms promise the same care. “For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone” (Psalm 91:11–12). “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them” (Psalm 34:7). Some take that angel as the chief of God’s angels; if he is the one who elsewhere speaks as God, the Son himself camps around his people. Either way the verb belongs to an army: God’s protection is not a feeling but a camp.

Eyes opened

When the Syrian army surrounded Elisha at Dothan, his servant cried out in fear. Elisha prayed, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see” (2 Kings 6:17). He did not ask God to send help. The help was already there: “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17). The servant’s problem was not that he was unprotected, but that he could not see it. The study Spiritual Warfare tells this story more fully.

Peter rescued, James taken

The most vivid rescue in the New Testament is told with striking honesty. King Herod “killed James the brother of John with the sword” (Acts 12:2), then arrested Peter to do the same. On the last night, with Peter chained between two soldiers, “an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell … And the chains fell off his hands” (Acts 12:7). The iron gate opened of its own accord, and in the street Peter said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me” (Acts 12:11).

But James was not rescued. Luke puts the two side by side and does not explain. The angels’ care is real, but it is no promise that harm will never touch a believer. When the devil quoted Psalm 91 to Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple, Jesus refused to test it (Matthew 4:5–7), and in the end he went where no angel rescued him, to the cross. The psalm was fulfilled for him on the far side of death. So it is for us. Angels may turn aside a danger we never knew was coming; they may also be sent for us on the day God calls us home.

Carried home

Jesus tells of a beggar who lay at a rich man’s gate, covered in sores, with dogs licking them. No one helped him while he lived. Then: “The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side” (Luke 16:22). It is a parable, and we should not press its details, but Jesus chose this one. The man nobody would help was carried by angels. For a believer, death is not a lonely walk into the dark.

Guardian angels?

Does each person, or each believer, have a guardian angel of his own? Christians have answered differently.

Many have said yes. Jerome, on Matthew 18:10, spoke of the dignity of souls, each with an angel appointed from birth to guard it. This is the common view in the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church, drawing on Basil of Caesarea, teaches that beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd. Many Protestants agree. They point to “their angels” in Matthew 18:10; to the church in Acts, which, when Rhoda said Peter was at the door, replied, “It is his angel!” (Acts 12:15); and to Daniel 10, where angelic princes seem to have charge of particular nations.

Others, including John Calvin and many in the Reformed tradition, are more cautious. Calvin dared not affirm that each believer has a single angel assigned to him, and thought it not worth anxious inquiry, since it is certain that all the angels together watch over our salvation. Acts 12:15 records what the praying church said in surprise, not what God revealed; and Jesus speaks of “their angels”, not “his angel”.

This commentary’s view: Scripture plainly teaches that God sends angels to serve his people, and especially the weak and the little, but it does not say that each person has exactly one, and a doctrine should not be built on a phrase spoken to make another point. The comfort does not lie in having an angel of our own. It lies in the Father who commands them all.

Comfort without speculation

So we do not pray to angels, try to see them or learn their names. Martin Luther’s morning prayer in the Small Catechism asks God to let his holy angel be with us, so that the evil foe may have no power over us. That is the right direction: we speak to the Father, through the Son, and leave the angels to him.

An example

An elderly widow, living alone since her husband died, began to dread the nights. Every noise in the house woke her. Her pastor read Psalm 34:7 and 2 Kings 6 with her. She still locks her doors, as she should. But she has started to pray before sleep, “Lord, open my eyes,” and to think of the house as a camp rather than a cage.

For reflection

Why does it matter that the mighty angels are sent to serve the weak? How does the story of Peter and James keep us from expecting the wrong things from God’s promises? Why is it wiser to pray to God about his angels than to seek them for ourselves?

5.title: Not Angels, but the Offspring of Abraham
5.essay:
Not all the angels stood. Some rebelled and fell, and God did not rescue them. Few truths in the Bible are more sobering. It is also the dark background against which the gospel shines brightest.

What we are told

Scripture says little about the fall of angels, and what it says is grave. “God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment” (2 Peter 2:4). Jude speaks of “the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling” (Jude 6). Paul warns that a proud new convert may “fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:6), which suggests that pride lay at the root.

Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 are often read as accounts of Satan’s fall; this commentary takes them as being about human kings, whose pride mirrors the devil’s. Whether the “sons of God” of Genesis 6 were fallen angels it leaves open. For the devil himself and Christ’s victory over him, see the study Spiritual Warfare. Here we look at one thing: what their fall tells us about grace.

No Saviour for angels

Jesus speaks of “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). Nowhere in Scripture is any redemption offered to them. No sacrifice was made for them, no gospel is preached to them, no call to repent ever reaches them. Hebrews says so in one quiet sentence: “For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham” (Hebrews 2:16).

The word translated “helps” means to take hold of. It is the word Matthew uses when Peter was sinking in the waves: “Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him” (Matthew 14:31). The Son of God reached past the angels, the higher creatures, and took hold of us.

Why us, and not them?

Scripture does not give a full answer, and we should be careful, but theologians have pointed out some differences. Humanity fell in one man, Adam, and so could be rescued in one man, the second Adam; the angels are not a race descended from one head, and each one that fell, fell for himself. Hebrews draws the link to the incarnation: “Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things” (Hebrews 2:14). To save angels the Son would have had to become an angel. He became a man.

But none of this makes us deserving. If anything, the angels who fell had less to drag them down than we did: as far as we are told, no tempter whispered to the first of them. The real answer is the one God gave Israel: “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you … but it is because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Grace cannot be explained by anything in those who receive it. That is what makes it grace.

Lower than the angels

Now see what the Son did. Hebrews quotes Psalm 8: “You made him for a little while lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:7). And then: “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9).

The Creator of the angels took a nature lower than theirs, and he did not lay it aside when the work was done. He rose in it and ascended in it. Today a human being, with a human body and human scars, sits at the right hand of God, “with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him” (1 Peter 3:22). The highest place in the universe is held by a man, and the angels bow to him. They see in him what God thought of the creatures they had been sent to serve.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that the gospel tells us we are more sinful and flawed than we ever dared believe, and at the same time more loved and accepted in Jesus Christ than we ever dared hope. The fall of the angels sharpens both halves. We are no better than they were. And we are loved as they were never loved: not more beautiful, not more deserving, only taken hold of.

What this means for us

It humbles us. We have no ground to look down on the fallen, for “but for grace” is the whole difference between us. It steadies us. Fallen angels are still creatures, already disarmed at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and Paul is sure that neither “angels nor rulers … nor powers … will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). And it fills us with wonder. The holy angels have watched God pass by the rebels of their own kind and stoop to rescue rebels of ours. No wonder they long to look into it.

An example

A woman who had walked away from Christ in her twenties came back, years later, convinced she had gone too far to be forgiven. She had read Hebrews 6 and feared it was about her. Her pastor showed her Hebrews 2:16. The ones Christ passed by were fallen angels; she was a human sinner, the very kind he came to take hold of, and he had promised, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). If such despair ever turns into thoughts of ending your life, tell someone the same day and call emergency services or a crisis line: you are not beyond his reach, and you are not meant to carry this alone.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Hebrews 2:16 uses the word for Jesus taking hold of sinking Peter? Why is it dangerous to think we were saved because we were more deserving than the angels who fell? What does it say about God that a human being now sits at his right hand? How might Hebrews 2:16 help someone who fears they are beyond forgiveness?

6.title: “Worship God”: Christ Far Above the Angels
6.essay:
Near the end of Revelation the apostle John, overwhelmed by what he had seen, fell at the feet of the angel who had shown it to him. He did it twice (Revelation 19:10; 22:8). If an apostle could be drawn to worship an angel, so can we. The angel’s answer tells us where worship belongs.

“You must not do that!”

The angel stopped him at once: “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God” (Revelation 22:9). A messenger of heaven calls himself John’s fellow servant. Holy angels are not jealous of their own honour; they are jealous for God’s, and their delight is to turn our eyes away from themselves.

That is why this commentary holds that there is to be no praying to angels or saints: prayer goes to God through Christ alone. The angels would have it no other way.

The trouble at Colossae

Paul warned the church at Colossae: “Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head” (Colossians 2:18–19). Scholars debate whether the false teachers were worshipping angels or claiming, in their visions, to join in the angels’ own worship. Either way, reaching for a higher spirituality, they were losing hold of Christ.

Paul’s answer in that letter is to make Christ big. He is the one by whom the thrones and authorities of heaven were made (Colossians 1:16), and the one who at the cross “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). Why look up to the servants when you belong to the King?

Hebrews 1: the Son and the angels

Hebrews opens with a long argument that the Son is greater than the angels. Its first readers seem to have been tempted to drift back from Christ to older ways, perhaps with an exaggerated regard for the angels through whom the law had come. The writer piles up seven quotations from the Old Testament, and each one draws a line between the Son and every angel.

He is “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3). “For to which of the angels did God ever say, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you’?” (Hebrews 1:5). Angels are made into winds and flames, servants of the moment (Hebrews 1:7), but to the Son God says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Hebrews 1:8), and, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning” (Hebrews 1:10). No angel was ever told to sit at God’s right hand (Hebrews 1:13).

And here is the decisive verse: “And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, ‘Let all God’s angels worship him’” (Hebrews 1:6). Put that beside Revelation 22:9. The angels refuse worship, because they are creatures. Yet God commands all the angels to worship the Son. There is only one way to hold those two verses together: the Son is not a creature. He is God. That is why the teaching of Jehovah’s Witnesses, that Jesus is Michael the archangel, cannot stand beside Hebrews 1. The archangel himself is among those commanded to bow.

“Even if … an angel from heaven”

Paul gave the Galatians a test for every messenger: “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8). The question is never how glorious the messenger looks. It is whether the message is the gospel of Christ. Paul also warns that “even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14).

This matters, because some great religious movements trace their beginnings to an angel. Latter-day Saints believe that the angel Moroni led Joseph Smith to the golden plates of the Book of Mormon. Muslims believe that the angel Gabriel brought the Qur’an to Muhammad. Those who hold these beliefs deserve to be spoken of with respect. But Paul’s words were written for exactly such a claim. A message that adds to the finished gospel of Christ, or denies that he is God, is not to be received, whoever brings it.

Angels in a spiritual age

In our day angels have become popular in a new way. There are angel cards for guidance, books on contacting your guardian angel and learning its name, and therapies that promise healing through angelic energies. It is worth asking gently why this appeals. An angel seems to offer the spiritual without the demands of a holy God: comfort without repentance, a being who serves me but never commands me.

The longing underneath is real. People want to know that they are not alone and that someone good is watching over them. But Scripture never tells us to seek angels, call on them or learn their names, and it forbids every attempt to gain guidance from spirits outside God’s word (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). The angels of the Bible would point every one of these seekers to the one they themselves worship. The good news is better than angel cards: the Lord of the angels has come near, by his Spirit, to all who trust him.

An example

A Christian nurse noticed that a colleague kept a deck of angel cards in her locker and drew one before every hard shift. She did not mock her. One quiet night she asked what the cards meant to her, and listened. Later she told her about the angel in Revelation who refused to be worshipped and said, “Worship God”, and about the Jesus whom all the angels worship. Her colleague was not persuaded that night, but she asked if they could talk again.

For reflection

Why do you think John, of all people, was tempted to worship an angel? How do Hebrews 1:6 and Revelation 22:9, taken together, show that Jesus is God? What is the test Galatians 1:8 gives for any spiritual message? How would you speak kindly but truthfully to a friend who is fascinated by angels?

7.title: Innumerable Angels in Festal Gathering
7.essay:
In the story of the Bible the angels usually come one or two at a time: to a tent, a prison cell, a garden tomb. At the end they will come all together, and believers will discover that they have a place in heaven’s company which no angel ever had.

With him at his coming

Jesus said, “When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne” (Matthew 25:31). Paul says he will be “revealed from heaven with his mighty angels” (2 Thessalonians 1:7), and that “the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Christ returns once, visibly and bodily, and the whole host of heaven with him.

They come to work. “He will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other” (Matthew 24:31). Not one of his people will be overlooked: not the martyr in an unmarked grave, not the believer forgotten in a care home, not the child who died before anyone knew her name.

They also come as reapers. In the parable of the weeds Jesus said, “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers” (Matthew 13:41). That is solemn, and the study Judgment and Hell treats it with the seriousness it deserves. But Jesus goes straight on: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43). The angels who clear the field are clearing it for a harvest of light.

We are to judge angels

Paul asked the quarrelling Corinthians, “Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!” (1 Corinthians 6:3). He most likely means the fallen angels, kept “until the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6). But the remark tells us something about the place of the redeemed. Hebrews says that “it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come” (Hebrews 2:5). It is given to man: to the Man Christ Jesus first, and in him to all who are his. Creatures made a little lower than the angels will share the reign of the one who was made lower than the angels for us.

Already in the festival

That sounds far off, but in a sense Hebrews says we have already arrived. It contrasts Sinai, where even Moses said, “I tremble with fear” (Hebrews 12:21), with the place to which the gospel brings us: “But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven … and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:22–24).

“You have come.” Not “you will come”. Whenever a church gathers in Jesus’ name, however small, it is joined by the Spirit to that assembly. And the angels there are “in festal gathering”: the word describes a festival crowd, a whole city out in the streets to celebrate. Sinai had fire and darkness and the trumpet. Zion has a festival, and Jesus is at the centre of it, with “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).

Side by side

Revelation shows the redeemed and the angels together. A great multitude from every nation cries, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10). Then “all the angels were standing around the throne … and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God” (Revelation 7:11), answering the multitude’s song with “Amen!” The ones who served us at every step will worship beside us, and they will not envy us. They rejoiced over each sinner who repented; on that day they will see them all at once.

Jesus said that the little ones’ angels “always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18:10). The last chapter of the Bible says of all God’s servants, “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). What the angels have always had as servants of the court, the children will have at last as sons and daughters of the house.

Every angel

At the centre of it all is the one we began with. “When he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, ‘Let all God’s angels worship him’” (Hebrews 1:6). Many have heard in those words the night of his birth, when a choir sang over a field; others hear his return. Either way, at the end it will be obeyed by all God’s angels, in one voice, “numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain’” (Revelation 5:11–12).

Think of who they are. The seraphim who cover their faces. Gabriel who stands in the presence of God. Michael the great prince. The angel who strengthened him in Gethsemane, the one who struck off Peter’s chains, the one who sat on the stone. Every one of them will bow before a man with scars in his hands, the one who made them all and then made himself lower than them all, for us. And we will be there, not as onlookers at the edge of the crowd, but as the ones for whom he was slain, close enough to see his face.

An example

A village chapel had dwindled to eleven members, most of them over seventy. One wet Sunday the preacher read Hebrews 12:22–24, looked round the half-empty room and said, “We are not eleven people this morning. We have come to the city of the living God.” An old farmer said afterwards that he had sung better that morning than he had in years.

For reflection

What comfort is there in knowing that the angels will gather every one of Christ’s people? How does Hebrews 12:22–24 change the way you think about your church’s gatherings? When you picture every angel bowing before the Lamb, what do you most want to say to him?
